The methodology section reports the PISA sampling scale (nearly 690,000 students across 81 economies; Wales: 2,568 students in 89 schools) and notes that not all questionnaire items were administered to every student, implying a complex survey design and planned missingness across questionnaire items. However, the excerpt does not specify whether PISA sampling weights (or replicate weights) were applied in the OECD/Wales comparisons, nor does it name any weight variables. For analysts replicating these comparisons, the recommended approach is to use the official PISA sampling weights and replicate weights provided with the PISA 2022 dataset when producing standard errors and confidence intervals; if weights are not applied, uncertainty estimates may be biased due to stratification and clustering at school and country levels.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PISA 2022 to describe teenage career development in Wales (students aged 15–16) and compares Wales to OECD averages, with additional trend context from PISA 2015 and 2018. The analysis is based on student questionnaire responses on career development activities and career thinking (e.g., career certainty/uncertainty, occupational expectations coded to ISCO, educational ambitions aligned to ISCED), alongside principal questionnaire information about how schools organise career guidance. In Wales, career uncertainty is high (44% uncertain in 2022 vs 39% across the OECD), and occupational expectations are strongly concentrated in professions (e.g., 63% of students with an occupational plan expect professional occupations, compared with 22.5% of actual workers aged 30–34). The paper also reports equity-related patterns (gender and social disparities) and highlights opportunity to increase engagement in career development activities, especially for disadvantaged and low-performing students. The excerpt does not report any ML modeling, PV estimation, or explicit missing-data strategy, so results should be interpreted as descriptive comparative evidence rather than model-based causal effects.
